 --> London's AQI is below 100, but PM2.5 levels are 5 times WHO guideline: What's behind the air pollution alert?
 Dense fog and low wind speeds allowed pollutants to accumulate across London over the weekend, prompting a high pollution warning. Here is why the city's AQI reading below 100 does not tell the full story about its air quality. 
 Moneycontrol World Desk 
 November 10, 2026 / 20:11 IST Share --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 People walk beside autumn foliage along the River Thames on a foggy morning in London, Britain, November 7, 2026. REUTERS/Toby Melville London issued a high air pollution alert due to PM2.5 levels exceeding WHO guidelines fivefold, driven by stagnant weather and festive emissions, despite an AQI of 76. Mayor Sadiq Khan urged residents to cut emissions and limit exposure. Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery

 London issued a high air pollution alert on Tuesday despite its overall Air Quality Index (AQI) remaining below 100, drawing attention to the elevated levels of fine particulate matter in the British capital. 
 According to aqicn.org, London's AQI stood at 76 at 5:28 pm IST on Tuesday. However, PM2.5 concentrations were around five times higher than the guideline level recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). 
 The alert followed a weekend of dense fog and very light winds, weather conditions that allowed pollutants to accumulate over London and remain in the air into Monday morning. UK government forecasters had predicted high particle pollution for Tuesday. 
 Imperial College London forecasters advised Mayor Sadiq Khan to issue the warning. Khan subsequently urged residents to limit activities that contribute to pollution and take precautions, particularly those belonging to vulnerable groups. 
 Why has London issued a high pollution alert despite AQI below 100? 
 Related Stories
 71% of Delhi's PM2.5 came from firecrackers after Diwali; know what IITM's new study reveals 
 Diwali pollution: AQI doubles in several state capitals, Delhi remains most polluted 
 The difference between London's overall AQI reading and its high pollution warning is linked to the concentration of specific pollutants, particularly PM2.5. 
 Fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, consists of tiny airborne particles that can enter the respiratory system. The WHO recommends a 24-hour mean concentration of no more than 15 micrograms per cubic metre for PM2.5. 
 London's PM2.5 levels were reported to be around five times this recommended guideline level, even as the overall AQI reading remained at 76. 
 Weather conditions also played a role. Dense fog and weak winds over the weekend restricted the dispersion of pollutants, allowing them to build up and linger over the city. 
 Emissions from Bonfire Night celebrations, Diwali fireworks and the burning of wood are also believed to have added to the pollution. 
 The alert was based on forecasts of high particle pollution rather than the overall AQI figure alone. 
 What precautions has London Mayor Sadiq Khan advised? 
 Alongside the pollution warning, Khan appealed to residents to reduce activities that contribute to emissions and limit their exposure to polluted air. 
 City Hall has recommended several measures, including: 
 Use public transport: Residents have been encouraged to walk, cycle and use public transport more often, while avoiding busy roads wherever possible. 
 Reduce private vehicle use: People have been advised to limit car journeys, share rides and switch off engines when stationary. 
 Maintain vehicles: Drivers have been urged to keep their vehicles properly maintained and adopt responsible driving practices. 
 Avoid burning garden waste: Residents should compost garden waste or take it to designated disposal centres instead of burning it. 
 Limit domestic burning: Unnecessary burning at home, including the use of wood burners and open fires, should be avoided. 
 London's City Hall issues air pollution alerts to residents, schools and borough authorities whenever moderate, high or very high pollution levels are forecast. 
 Warnings are also displayed at public locations across the capital, including bus stop countdown signs and the Underground network, to inform commuters and other residents about changing air quality conditions. 
 London Deputy Mayor warns of health impact of air pollution 
 Deputy Mayor for Environment and Energy Mete Coban highlighted the public health consequences of prolonged exposure to polluted air and called for collective efforts to reduce emissions. 
 “Toxic air is responsible for thousands of premature deaths in London each year, which is why the Mayor has done everything in his power to tackle it, which includes launching the world’s largest clean air zone," Coban said. 
 He added that residents also had a role to play in protecting vulnerable people as London continued its efforts to create a safer and greener city. 
 The warning comes as London continues to address pollution through measures such as its clean air zone, alongside public advisories intended to reduce emissions and exposure during periods of deteriorating air quality.
